Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe (left) with Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya

The Asia/Pacific Group on Money Laundering (APG) yesterday held the inaugural meeting of Sri Lanka’s Third Mutual Evaluation on Anti-Money Laundering, Countering the Financing of Terrorism and Countering Proliferation Financing (AML/CFT/CPF), with Prime Minister Dr. Harini Amarasuriya stressing that the credibility of the country’s financial system would be judged on how its safeguards work in practice.

A mutual evaluation is a peer review of how effectively a country prevents its financial system from being used to launder money and to finance terrorism and the spread of weapons of mass destruction.

“The strength of a country’s financial system depends not only on the institutions and regulations it puts in place, but also on how effectively they work together in practice,” Dr. Amarasuriya said.

She said the evaluation provided an important opportunity for Sri Lanka to demonstrate its progress in combating financial crime, identify areas requiring further improvement and strengthen alignment with international standards.

Dr. Amarasuriya warned that corruption and the erosion of public trust in State institutions, particularly financial institutions, posed significant challenges to economic and political stability. Addressing these through transparency, accountability, strong institutional coordination and effective enforcement was essential to safeguarding financial integrity, restoring public confidence and strengthening the country’s economic resilience, she said.

She reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to working constructively with the assessment team and all relevant stakeholders to strengthen Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT/CPF framework, address emerging risks and uphold the confidence of international partners and investors, the Prime Minister’s Media Division said.

The meeting was attended by Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eranga Weeraratne, Central Bank Governor Dr. Nandalal Weerasinghe, the Secretary to the Minister of Justice and National Integration, members of the Financial Intelligence Unit and members of the assessment team.

From left: Lak Jaya Microfinance CEO Nimesh Fernando, Berendina Micro Investments Company CEO Charith Fernando, Lanka Microfinance Practitioners’ Association President Wasantha Gunawardena, CRIB Director/General Manager Pushpike Jayasundera, CBSL Director Supervision of NBFI R.M.C.H.K. Jayasinghe,  Dumbara Micro Credit CEO Gnanasiri Abeywardena and Sejaya Micro Credit CEO Rizanth Francis

Chief Guest CRIB Chairman and Central Bank Deputy Governor K.G.P. Sirikumara

The Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka (CRIB) has announced a significant expansion of the country’s credit information ecosystem with the onboarding of four licenced microfinance institutions, following the publication of the relevant Government Gazette Notification.

This initiative marks an important step towards strengthening credit information sharing within the microfinance sector, enhancing the availability of reliable credit information, and promoting greater financial inclusion by facilitating improved access to formal credit for underserved individuals and businesses.

Under the powers vested in the Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka Act, No. 18 of 1990, four Licenced Microfinance Companies have been formally declared as designated lending institutions. The newly included institutions are Berendina Micro Investments Company Ltd., Lak Jaya Micro Finance Ltd., Dumbara Micro Credit Ltd., and Sejaya Micro Credit Ltd.

This regulatory inclusion integrates microfinance institutions into CRIB’s centralised credit information infrastructure, enabling them to both contribute credit information and access borrower profiles within a secure and well-governed framework. This development will strengthen the institutions’ capacity to expand their reach to underserved and marginalised segments of the economy by improving the visibility of data and supporting more informed lending decisions. Furthermore, access to reliable credit information will help these institutions strengthen credit risk assessment, enhance risk management practices, uphold sound governance standards, and promote responsible lending, thereby facilitating wider access to formal credit and supporting sustainable economic empowerment.

A ceremony to mark the onboarding of microfinance data to CRIB was held recently with the participation of CRIB Chairman and Central Bank Deputy Governor K.G.P. Sirikumara as the chief guest, CBSL Director Department of Supervision of Non-Bank Financial Institutions R. M. C. H. K. Jayasinghe, CRIB Director/General Manager Pushpike Jayasundera, Lanka Microfinance Practitioners’ Association President Wasantha Gunawardhane, Chief Executive Officers of the respective companies, other officials of the companies and CRIB.

Commenting on the development, Pushpike Jayasundera said: “The formal integration of licenced microfinance companies into the CRIB framework marks a pivotal step toward building a truly inclusive financial ecosystem in Sri Lanka. Microfinance plays a vital role in supporting micro-entrepreneurs, small businesses, and grass-roots economic activity. By bringing these institutions into our national credit intelligence network, we are mitigating information asymmetry at the micro level, encouraging responsible borrowing, and enabling financial institutions to extend credit with greater risk confidence.”

The inclusion of these institutions aligns with CRIB’s broader strategic objective to expand credit coverage beyond mainstream commercial banking into grassroots and micro-finance sectors, further driving financial inclusion, credit discipline, and sustainable economic revitalisation across Sri Lanka.

Established by the Credit Information Bureau of Sri Lanka Act No. 18 of 1990 as amended by Act No. 8 of 1995 and 42 of 2008, CRIB is the first credit bureau in the South Asian region. An initiative of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka and the Ministry of Finance, the Bureau serves as the national repository of credit information for all borrowers, delivering a range of value-added services that facilitate faster and more affordable access to credit, thereby enhancing financial inclusion for all citizens.

title: Sri Lanka aims to be South Asia’s Fintech Hub | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:03
-     - 64

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne

Digital Economy Deputy Minister Eng. Eranga Weeraratne believes fintech will play a key role in moving Sri Lanka from a cash-heavy to a cash-light economy. Ahead of the Sri Lanka FinTech Festival 2026, organised by the FinTech Forum Sri Lanka with the Ministry and scheduled at Shangri-La Colombo from 2-3 November, he reiterated the Ministry’s vision for the event, the investment and policy changes under way, and plans to make Sri Lanka a regional fintech hub.

Q: What is the Ministry’s vision for the Sri Lanka FinTech Festival 2026, and how can the event help position Sri Lanka as a competitive fintech hub in the global digital economy?

A: When the Ministry was established, we identified digital payments as one of the key pillars of the country’s digitalisation. Sri Lanka is a very cash-heavy society, with about Rs. 1.48 trillion in circulation as notes and coins, and more than 99% of retail transactions still happen in cash. People withdraw cash and then transact in cash, so many sectors remain informal. We want a more formal industrial and SME sector and moving from cash heavy to cash light is our ambition. 

Fintech will play a key role in the transformation. Our target is to involve the private sector more in the Government and country digitalisation, because banks, formal financial institutions and fintech companies can provide the digital payment rails the country needs.

We do not have to reinvent everything. India, Singapore, Kenya and others offer successful case studies, and an event such as this, it brings foreign expertise into the country so we can learn from it. It also lets us showcase our success stories to the world, ensuring Sri Lankan companies gain international exposure and access to international markets.

Q: The festival brings together policymakers, startups, investors, and established financial institutions. How important is cross-industry collaboration in accelerating innovation and shaping the future of Sri Lanka’s financial services sector?

A: Formal financial institutions and private sector fintech companies need to work together. Current policy frameworks may have to change in order for fintech organisations to provide more independent services, and we are looking at that policy change. It would also let them provide more public services, from payment rails to tap-and-go, and card-based solutions. We need foreign industry players to come to the country and work with local industry to deliver these services.

Existing financial institutions will continue to dominate the space. What we need is a bridge between traditional financial models and fintech models, and it is where technology companies add value. Fintech companies are agile. Therefore, their transformation will be much faster than traditional institutions. We need the right balance between the two to accelerate the shift.

Q: As Sri Lanka advances its digital economy, how does the Ministry plan to ensure that fintech innovation translates into greater financial inclusion, particularly for rural communities and underserved populations?

A: There are several benefits to a cash-light society. We currently spend about 1.5% of GDP on handling cash, from printing and secure transport to storage and management. Digital payments bring the cost down, and transactions become more transparent because revenue is recorded and maintained digitally.

The informal sector also becomes more formal. When micro, small and medium businesses move to digital payments, they adopt formal cash management and cashless accounting practices. Their business history can then justify funding from formal financial institutions, which makes them more investable and lifts the whole economy. It also includes rural communities and underserved populations.

The Government is also moving towards e-invoicing, collected centrally over digital rails. To achieve this, SMEs and other businesses need to use ERP and point-of-sale systems, which is much needed to make e-invoicing work.

Q: What competitive advantages and investment opportunities can Sri Lanka offer to global investors attending the festival, and how can these be leveraged to attract foreign investment and scale the country’s digital economy?

A: There are two sides to it. First, we are looking for foreign direct investment into digital platforms in Sri Lanka. Although certain payments are already available, we have much more to develop, from smart cards to tap-and-go payments, and we invite foreign investors to invest in them. 

Second, some solid fintech solutions have been developed here, and we can offer our experience, expertise and solutions to other countries, because many markets are still behind Sri Lanka. Approaching those markets is also part of the exercise.

To attract investors, we will showcase the economic opportunity in the country, including the gaps, and speak openly about the Government’s vision and policy. We will also market our digital workforce, products and solutions, thereby foreign investors can invest in our products, intellectual property and companies, and help open markets abroad.

Q: How is the Ministry working with fintech startups, banks, and other financial institutions to foster an enabling environment for innovation, entrepreneurship, and the wider adoption of digital financial services?

A: There are multiple initiatives. We run start-up development programs covering incubation and facilitation, and Disrupt Asia, a conference to connect start-ups with investors. We are also setting up a fund of funds, a Government sovereign fund, to support research and development and start-ups to create more intellectual property in the country. Our strategy is to keep startups headquarters in Sri Lanka allowing companies to grow internationally.

The fund will be a matching funding scheme for foreign investors who invest in Sri Lanka, run by an independent fund manager. The policy papers are in the final stage, and next year’s Budget will include an allocation to facilitate it.

Q: What key regulatory, policy, and digital infrastructure developments are underway to strengthen Sri Lanka’s fintech ecosystem, build investor confidence, and accelerate the country’s digital transformation?

A: With the Fund of Funds, we also see a gap in the regulatory environment for fund management. Foreign and local funds are currently set up as private limited companies under the Companies Act, which means double taxation and capital movement restrictions. For a fund to operate properly, we must provide tax pass-through and capital mobility. We are therefore bringing in a qualified venture company funding scheme as a regulatory framework, most likely with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which we would like to see as the regulatory body for fund management. Policy development is under way and we expect to have it in place from next year.

We will also establish special virtual economic zones, which will allow foreign institutions to set up virtually in Sri Lanka and use supporting services from here, and at the same time operating under the Sri Lankan Government framework. 

On digital infrastructure, we have invited foreign hyperscalers to establish cloud infrastructure and AI data centres in the country, and we see tremendous interest from those investors. We are evaluating the expressions of interest received and will publish a baseline of the facilities the Government is willing to provide. We will then discuss with individual investors how to attract them and set up the data centres here. The strategy is for these data centres to serve not only local demand but also to make Sri Lanka an AI and data centre hub for the region.

Q: Can the festival help position Sri Lanka as a regional hub for future fintech and events?

A: Sri Lanka can be a fintech festival hub for South Asia. We are going to expand the festival into a regional event, with the aim of attracting more foreign participants to showcase their solutions here. It would also help make Sri Lanka a MICE hub, and fintech is a very attractive proposition in that sense, from the Gulf to Singapore.

title: FASL outlines contributions since 2018; seeks clarity on AFA membership selection | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:02
-     - 41

FASL Founding President Rajkumar Kanagasingam (second from left) and then Singapore FinTech Association President Chia Hock Lai exchange an MoU in April 2019, witnessed by the then Central Bank of Sri Lanka Assistant Governor R. A. Ananda Jayalath and other representatives

The Fintech Association of Sri Lanka (FASL) has issued the following statement in response to comments by LankaPay CEO and FinTech Forum Sri Lanka Chairman Channa de Silva in the Daily FT interview published on 22 October 2026, “FinTech Forum to connect fintechs, build trust and open doors abroad.”

In the interview, Channa de Silva states that AFA selected FinTech Forum as its sole member association from Sri Lanka. He also says the Forum provides fintech companies with a channel to engage the Central Bank and Government that they previously lacked.

Although FASL is not named, the interview indirectly questions the achievements of earlier association initiatives. FASL therefore provides context on its contributions and the outstanding AFA membership questions.

Contributions since 2018

Established and incorporated in 2018, FASL has developed regional partnerships, supported entrepreneurs, contributed to research and education, and advanced international engagement.

In April 2019, FASL signed an MoU with the Singapore FinTech Association at Mandarin Oriental, Singapore.

In June 2019, FASL signed an MoU with the FinTech Association of Hong Kong. Signatories included its then General Manager Syed Musheer Ahmed, with Professor Douglas W. Arner, Kerry Holdings Professor in Law at the University of Hong Kong, among the witnesses.

FASL’s partnerships also include fintech associations in Japan and the Philippines. In March 2024, it signed an MoU with the Indonesian Fintech Association (AFTECH), in Colombo.

FASL’s Singapore FinTech Festival Community Partner role dates back to 2019, while supporting engagement with Hong Kong FinTech Week is documented from 2020.

FASL was named a Community Partner of Seamless Middle East in 2020, with engagement through 2024 encompassing institutional support, speaking contributions and participation on judging panels. It has also served as an Association Partner of the Dubai FinTech Summit for the 2024, 2025 and 2026 editions. Wider engagements include Global FinTech Fest in Mumbai and platforms in Vietnam, Shanghai and Hong Kong.

Supporting ventures and innovation

As a collaborating partner of the 2019 FinX Awards in Dubai, FASL helped connect Sri Lankan startups with international opportunities. Helios P2P participated in the Al Baraka challenge, while iLoan was selected for the Emirates NBD challenge.

In 2020, FASL became a strategic partner of HatchX, the fintech accelerator launched by Hatch and the Lankan Angel Network with Ford Foundation support and Central Bank endorsement.

In April 2021, FASL signed an MoU with the ASEAN Financial Innovation Network to promote fintech development through APIX. Further collaboration was announced in 2026.

FASL initiated a report on enhancing Port City Colombo as a leading South Asian fintech hub, with Professor Arner as Chief Consultant. An interim report was presented in 2024 to then Commission Chairman Dinesh Weerakkody and then Monetary Authority of Singapore Chief FinTech Officer Sopnendu Mohanty.

FASL organised FinTech World Cup Regional Competitions at Port City Colombo in 2025 and 2026. AnybanQ.lk progressed to the 2025 Dubai global final; RealX and NanoSoft Global jointly won the 2026 regional competition.

FASL’s knowledge activities include awareness workshops and contributions acknowledged in the 2022 Global COVID-19 Fintech Market Impact and Industry Resilience Study, jointly published by the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, the World Bank and the World Economic Forum. It served as Knowledge Partner for the Asian Digital Finance Forum & Awards in 2022 and 2023 and as co-organiser in 2025.

AFA’s clarification and outstanding questions

Following private correspondence, FASL published its representation query on 6 October 2026.

On 13 October, AFA Chairwoman Jaclyn Tsai confirmed its one-member-association-per-jurisdiction framework and FinTech Forum Sri Lanka’s membership.

She clarified that membership does not designate an association as the sole or exclusive representative of an entire national fintech ecosystem, nor diminish other associations’ standing.

FASL welcomes this clarification. Its separate selection questions remain outstanding:

What eligibility and assessment criteria applied?

Was FASL’s institutional record considered?

How could established associations submit credentials before the membership position was filled?

Is a review mechanism or alternative participation pathway available? 

The Daily FT interview identifies capability, membership, constitution and governance as factors in AFA’s membership assessment. However, FASL was neither approached nor invited to submit its credentials before the Sri Lankan member was selected. FASL has therefore asked AFA how potential associations were identified, how these criteria were applied and whether FASL’s record was considered. These questions remain unanswered at the time of this statement.

Sri Lanka’s fintech development reflects contributions from multiple institutions. Public discussion should recognise those contributions and distinguish membership of a private alliance from an exclusive national mandate.

The Business Promotion Mission of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce in Sri Lanka (CanCham Sri Lanka) is creating opportunities for its member companies to connect with Canadian investors, explore commercial partnerships and expand their reach to international markets. 

Running from 18 October to 1 November 2026, the mission travels across Vancouver, Toronto, Ottawa and Montréal, with a focus on sectors such as tourism, real estate and infrastructure, AgriTech, green housing, healthcare and wellness, education, IT and Fintech, with Women in Development and Empowerment identified as a special area of interest.

Building a Canada–Sri Lanka–Indo-Pacific business corridor

At a business conclave and networking session in Vancouver hosted by Surrey Board of Trade former President and CEO Anita Huberman, CanCham Sri Lanka Co-Founder and Board Director Mohamed Hameez outlined the Chamber’s proposed Canada–Sri Lanka–Indo-Pacific Corridor Initiative. 

“Our proposed initiative seeks to connect Canadian expertise, capital and innovation with Sri Lanka’s capabilities and commercial opportunities. At a time of changing global trade dynamics, market diversification is increasingly important. Sri Lanka’s strategic location at the crossroads of South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Middle East, together with its position along major maritime routes, presents opportunities for Canadian businesses seeking to expand their reach into regional markets,” he said. 

The initiative is intended to link Canadian investment and expertise with Sri Lankan businesses and resources, providing a framework for exploring commercial cooperation across the two countries and the wider Indo-Pacific.

Connecting member companies with Canadian investors

Representing a range of sectors including property development, education, telecommunications, tourism and manufacturing, the delegation comprises members of Home Lands Skyline, Port City Colombo, Horizon Campus, Horizon College International, Hutch Sri Lanka, ECD Global, AmmA Mega Industries Ltd., Thames International Educational Consultancy and Spillburg Vacation Ltd.

The Vancouver program included meetings with colleges and universities, as well as Sri Lankan university student groups from British Columbia and Alberta, opening discussions on educational links and potential areas of collaboration. 

At the Port City Colombo Investment Forum – Metro Vancouver, Hameez highlighted Port City Colombo’s potential to attract regional business operations and investment. The forum connected Canadian investors with Sri Lankan business leaders to explore prospects in the country’s flagship Special Economic Zone. Former Surrey Councillor Linda Annis was also appointed CanCham Sri Lanka’s Honorary Brand Ambassador, which strengthens a further link between the Chamber and the Canadian community as it develops its international business network.

Advancing the mission across Canada

Following the Vancouver program, the delegation continues its mission in Toronto, Ottawa and Montréal, with further business, investment, institutional and tourism-related engagements planned across the three cities. 

CanCham Sri Lanka is also connected to investment-promotion initiatives in Sri Lanka, including the Northern Investment Summit and Sri Lanka Expo 2027. These platforms promote the Chamber’s international outreach by strengthening links between local enterprises and overseas investors. 

Through its involvement, CanCham Sri Lanka aims to build on its international business network and expand opportunities for international commercial cooperation.

title: WNPS goes to Court over guns for civilians as elephant killings rise | Daily FT

The Wildlife and Nature Protection Society (WNPS), Sri Lanka’s oldest and leading conservation organisation, had initiated legal action in the Court of Appeal to halt the State-issuance of firearms to civilians, which is driving an unprecedented surge in the slaughter of the country’s wild elephants.

The writ application seeks urgent judicial intervention to stop the escalating killing of elephants both within and outside protected reservations. WNPS argued in its Petition that the crisis had intensified following the relevant public authorities’ decision to issue firearms to civilians for the purpose of protecting crops from wild animals.

The legal challenge was filed in August 2025, over a year before the tragic and widely publicised killing of the iconic tusker ‘Kavantissa’. WNPS contends that this legal action should have served as a stark warning to the Department of Wildlife Conservation (DWC), the Ministry of Defence, Ministry of Environment, and other state authorities that placing firearms in civilian hands would inevitably result in the death of wild elephants, which are strictly protected under Sri Lankan law.

In its petition, WNPS highlighted the agonising death of another iconic tusker, ‘Bathiya’, who succumbed to multiple gunshot wounds after prolonged suffering in a pool of mud. The petition noted that Bathiya’s slow death exposed severe resource shortages and a critical lack of capacity within the DWC and local veterinary services to handle such wildlife emergencies. Strikingly, just a year later, the nation and the global conservation community witnessed the majestic tusker ‘Kavantissa’ perish under identical, preventable circumstances.

To underscore the staggering scale of the risk, the petition cited a statement made in Parliament on March 18, 2025, by MP Namal Karunaratne, revealing that the Government had distributed 13,207 firearms to farmers under the scheme. Subsequent court disclosures indicated that an extremely large number of  these State-issued weapons remained entirely unlicensed, and unaccounted for, presenting an existential threat to Sri Lanka’s endangered wildlife and national heritage.

Demonstrating a clear link between the distribution of weapons and rising violence against wild elephants, WNPS cited official figures published by the State, including the statement made by the Minister of Environment that 21 wild elephants had been shot in various locations within seven months in the period January to July, 2025, with most struck below the knee.

The petition emphasised that shootings account for approximately 20% of annual elephant deaths in Sri Lanka, pushing the endangered species closer to extinction. The Petition quotes the following profound observation made by His Lordship, Justice N.E. Dissanayake, Retired Supreme Court Judge in an in an inquiry report: “When the birth rate of elephants is considered with the annual rate of death of elephants it is clear that there is a grave threat of depletion of its numbers. You need not be a great mathematician to conclude that the day will not be too far away for our elephants to become extinct”.

WNPS further argued that releasing over 13,000 firearms to civilians (including where a large volume thereof remained unlicensed and unaccounted for), was an irrational and short-sighted measure, that directly contradicts the Government’s own law enforcement initiatives to seize illegal weapons and combat underworld crime. WNPS maintains that the indiscriminate distribution of firearms undermines the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance (FFPO), transforms a conservation crisis into a public safety hazard, and threatens the survival of Sri Lanka’s natural heritage.

In 2020, WNPS challenged the Sri Lankan Government’s issuance of 6,000 firearms to Civil Defence Forces to combat human-elephant conflict. This legal action led to the Hon. Attorney General representing the relevant public authorities, furnishing a formal undertaking before the Court of Appeal that the weapons would be recalled and the management of wildlife transferred to the Department of Wildlife Conservation. Despite this court undertaking and formal commitment, the relevant public authorities have repeatedly recycled this failed action, resulting in a continuous cycle of weapon distribution and escalating elephant fatalities.

Through this application, WNPS has urgently invited and moved for judicial intervention to protect Sri Lanka’s iconic national heritage from an unprecedented existential threat.

The Sri Lankan elephant is now listed as endangered by the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and faces imminent extinction. 

The Parliament of Sri Lanka has explicitly declared the Sri Lankan Elephant as Protected Public Property in terms of the provisions of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, rendering any harm caused to this national heritage a serious criminal offense met with the absolute harshest legal penalties.

WNPS remains steadfastly committed to safeguarding Sri Lanka’s majestic wild elephants and ensuring their survival for generations to come.

Following an application for contempt of court filed by Transparency International Sri Lanka (TISL) on 12 October 2026, the Supreme Court made directions on the failure of respondents in a medical procurement case to comply with its judgment requiring payment of Rs. 275 million in total, to the State.

The proceedings arise from the Supreme Court’s judgment delivered in case SC/FR/65/2023 on the 27 of March 2026, which found that five respondents; including former Health Minister Keheliya Rambukwella, former Health Secretary S. J. S. Chandraguptha, and three other senior officials had infringed the fundamental right to equal protection of the law guaranteed under Article 12(1) of the Constitution. The Court ordered the former Minister to pay Rs. 75 million to the State and each of the other four respondents to pay Rs. 50 million.

TISL subsequently moved the Supreme Court for contempt proceedings, alleging wilful disobedience of the judgment and seeking appropriate action since the payments remained outstanding seven months after the judgement was delivered.

At the hearing on Monday, the third respondent, former National Medicines Regulatory Authority (NMRA) Chairman Prof. S. D. Jayaratne submitted to Court that the payment of Rs. 50 million has been made on 22 October, following the filing of TISL’s contempt application. 

The remaining respondents undertook to make payments in the following manner:

*The first respondent, Rambukwella, made a payment of Rs. 20 million on 23 October 2026 and gave an undertaking to pay the outstanding balance of Rs. 55 million within two weeks.

*The second respondent, Chandraguptha, gave an undertaking to pay Rs. 5 million within a week and to settle the remaining Rs. 45 million within three months.

*The fourth respondent, former Chief Executive Officer of the NMRA Dr. Vijith Gunasekara gave an undertaking to pay Rs. 20 million within two weeks and the remaining Rs. 30 million within three months.

*The fifth respondent, former Medical Supplies Division Director Dr. A. Thusitha Sudharshana gave an undertaking to pay all his savings amounting to approximately Rs. 2 million within this week and to settle the outstanding balance of Rs. 48 million within three months.

The Supreme Court, while directing the first, second, fourth and fifth respondents to pay the total amounts due within three months, imposed travel bans on all four respondents. 

The Court ordered that they be enlarged on bail with each subject to a cash bond of Rs. 50 million and two sureties who must establish their capacity to pay the specified amount. The respondents were directed to fulfil the bail conditions within one week.

By bringing the non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s payment order before the Court, TISL sought to ensure that the Court’s orders were respected and that appropriate action was taken in response to their continued failure to be held accountable. 

TISL emphasises that compliance with judicial orders is fundamental to the rule of law and constitutional accountability. Such compliance must not be dependent on the petitioner’s ability to initiate further proceedings in Court. 

TISL further emphasises the following realities to those in positions of public power; their actions carry ethical and legal obligations towards the public they serve. Consequences of corruption carries long-term legal ramifications and permanent reputational harm. Civil Society Organisations and accountability actors will continue to actively monitor decisions to ensure strict adherence to legal frameworks and accountability standards.

Senior Counsel Senany Dayaratne with Attorneys-at-Law Lasanthika Hettiarachchi, Nishadi Wickramasinghe, Janani Abeywickrema and Maheshika Bandara appeared for TISL, instructed by Attorney-at-Law Thushari Jayawardena. The matter is fixed to be taken up on 15 February 2027.

title: From consumption to capacity: Taxing those who can pay | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:26
-     - 33

The World Bank has said what many Sri Lankan taxpayers have long felt. In a recent interview, World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel said Sri Lanka’s tax system should be progressive and simple, and focused primarily on taxing those who can most afford to pay. He also called for broadening the base, widening the tax net, and moving from indirect taxes towards direct taxes.

The timing matters. As Budget 2027 approaches, the question is no longer whether Sri Lanka needs more revenue. The question now is who should pay it, and how.

First phase was necessary

In 2022, Sri Lanka was collecting only around 7–8% of GDP in revenue, while even low-income countries were moving towards 15%. Under the IMF-backed reform program. VAT and income taxes were raised and exemptions were cut back. These measures were painful, but they were needed to restore fiscal stability.

The results are clear in the Finance Ministry’s Final Budget Position Report 2025. Tax revenue rose to Rs. 5,049.2 billion in 2025, or 15.4% of GDP, up from 12.3% in 2024. 

The World Bank accepts this. It also makes the more important point: revenue has risen very quickly, and the task now is to make it sustainable. Revenue that depends on squeezing the same compliant taxpayers is not sustainable. It is borrowed time.

Imbalance we cannot ignore

Indirect taxes still account for the bulk of collections, and the Ministry’s own figures show the gap is widening rather than narrowing. Direct taxes made up 33.5% of total tax revenue in 2023. That fell to 27.7% in 2024 and to just 22.6% in 2025, leaving indirect taxes with 77.4% of the total.

The composition tells the same story. In 2025, income tax brought in Rs. 1,139.4 billion, or 3.5% of GDP. Taxes on goods and services brought in Rs. 3,198.1 billion, or 9.8% of GDP, almost three times as much. VAT alone raised Rs. 1,746.9 billion, well above total income tax collections. Part of the 2025 shift reflects one-off factors such as excise duty on motor vehicles, which rose to Rs. 471.8 billion from Rs. 58.6 billion in 2024 as vehicle imports resumed. Even so, the long-term direction is clear: revenue growth is coming mainly from consumption.

VAT and similar levies are paid by every consumer at the same rate, whatever their income. A daily wage earner buying essentials and a high-net-worth individual buying luxuries add to the same pool, but the burden weighs far more heavily on the first.

Indirect taxes are efficient to collect, and no modern system can do without them. But when a tax system leans too heavily on consumption, it becomes regressive almost by default. It also weakens something harder to measure but essential to revenue: public trust.

Real gap is compliance, not rates

Perhaps the most telling part of the World Bank’s comments is the observation that a large number of people are not complying, and that significant leakages remain in the base, in compliance, and in administration.

This is the heart of the matter. Sri Lanka does not mainly have a rate problem; it has a coverage problem. The number of registered taxpayers grew to around 1.3 million in 2025, which is real progress. But registration is not the same as contribution. Salaried employees have tax deducted at source. Registered businesses file, pay, and get audited. Meanwhile, a significant share of people with real economic capacity, such as owners of multiple properties, high-value professionals operating informally, and those whose lifestyles clearly exceed their declared income, remain partly or entirely outside the net. The burden falls on registered businesses too as reflected in the World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025, 27.5% of business owners and top managers of 607 firms reported competing against unregistered or informal firms.

When the compliant few carry the load for the non-compliant many, every further rate increase deepens the unfairness. Taxing those who can pay is not about raising rates. It is about finding those who should already be paying.

Practical steps for next phase

Several measures could turn the World Bank’s principle into practice.

Use the data that already exists

Land registries, motor vehicle registrations, bank interest records, high-value transactions and foreign travel data together show a great deal about economic capacity. Systematically matching this information against tax filings would identify people who can pay but do not file, without adding any new tax.

Link the TIN to economic activity

The Government has already introduced the process requiring a Taxpayer Identification Number for major transactions, such as property transfers, high-value vehicle purchases and large investments, which would steadily draw capacity into the net and leaves an audit trail.

Shift the mix gradually

Moving from indirect to direct taxation should be sequenced, not sudden. With indirect taxes now making up more than three-quarters of tax revenue, a sharp cut in VAT or other consumption taxes would put the hard-won fiscal gains at risk. The shift should instead be tied to results. As income tax compliance improves and the base widens, the extra revenue should be used to ease the burden on consumption, for example by reviewing levies on essential goods or gradually phasing out overlapping taxes such as the SSCL which is a cascading tax in nature. Announcing this link in advance would make the commitment credible. That way, honest taxpayers see that compliance brings relief, not just more obligations.

Remove taxes that hold back growth

The World Bank has again called for moving away from distortionary taxes, especially para-tariffs, towards taxes that do not hold back private sector activity. A cleaner, simpler tax structure is both a growth measure and a compliance measure.

Make administration easier

In the World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025, which interviewed business owners and top managers of 607 firms, tax rates ranked as the single biggest obstacle to doing business cited by 19.3%. Tax administration came third at 12.3%, nearly three times the South Asian average of 4.6%. Together, almost one in three named tax as their biggest constraint.

Much of this burden can be eased without giving up revenue. Simplified returns, using shorter or pre-filled forms for both individuals and SMEs, would reduce compliance costs and honest errors. Predictable rulings, published on time, would give businesses certainty and prevent disputes. Faster refunds within set timelines, with interest paid on delays, would show that obligations run both ways. Consistent assessments would ensure compliant taxpayers are not targeted simply because they are easy to reach. None of these costs much in revenue, yet each does a great deal for the willingness to comply.

The need for Tax Ombudsman

The steps above, particularly data matching and TIN linkage, will give the Inland Revenue Department far greater visibility and reach. As the Government tightens tax administration and the Department is given stronger powers to access data, assess and collect, there must be an equally strong safeguard for taxpayers. An independent Tax Ombudsman would provide that. It would give taxpayers an accessible, low-cost avenue to raise complaints about delays, unfair treatment or the improper use of powers, without having to resort to lengthy appeals or litigation. Enhanced powers are necessary to reach those outside the net, but they must be applied consistently and within their intent, so that the honest taxpayers already in the net do not bear the cost of reaching those outside it. 

A Tax Ombudsman would bring transparency and accountability to the process and reassure taxpayers that stronger enforcement will be matched by fair treatment. As the system becomes stricter, an ombudsman is needed more than ever before.

Protect taxpayer data

The approach outlined above depends on the tax administration holding more information about taxpayers than ever before. Returns capture details of assets and liabilities, bank balances are reported through banking channels, and property ownership and transfers are drawn from the land registry etc. This is highly sensitive information, and the Government must ensure that it is protected with the same seriousness with which it is collected. Strong data privacy measures are needed, including strict controls on who can access taxpayer information and for what purpose, secure systems, clear audit trails of access, and meaningful consequences for any unauthorised use or disclosure. 

Taxpayers must be able to trust that the information they provide will be used only for tax purposes and kept secure. That trust is what will allow them to rely on the system. Without it, the very data that is meant to widen the net may instead drive people further away from it.

The Government’s new Medium-Term Revenue Strategy, which aims to close compliance gaps in VAT, income tax and other areas, provides the framework. What matters now is whether it is implemented consistently.

Fairness as revenue strategy

Tax morale, meaning a citizen’s willingness to pay, is shaped by what people see. When people see that those with visible wealth are paying their share, compliance rises. When they see the opposite, even honest taxpayers begin to question why they should stay in the system.


That is why the World Bank’s message goes beyond economic advice. A progressive, simple tax system focused on capacity to pay is fairer. It is also more resilient, because it rests on a broad base rather than on the patience of a narrow one.

Road ahead

Sri Lanka has done the hard part of raising revenue in a crisis. The next phase is harder in a different way. It requires data, administrative discipline and political will to reach those who have stayed outside the net.

Budget 2027 is an opportunity to signal that change, from taxing what people consume to taxing what they can afford. If we get this right, the reward will be more than revenue. It will be a tax system that citizens see as fair and are therefore more willing to support.

(This article draws on the recent interview given by World Bank Senior Economist Jakob Engel, World Bank’s Sri Lanka Enterprise Survey 2025 (country profile) published in April 2026 and on the Ministry of Finance’s Final Budget Position Report 2025. The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in her personal capacity)

title: Beyond promises on paper: Sri Lanka must deliver on investments it wins | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:24
-     - 39

In January 2025, Sri Lanka signed an agreement with Sinopec for a $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota, which remains on paper

Several years have passed since Sri Lanka faced the most severe economic crisis in its history. Macroeconomic stability has largely been restored, and the country is now nearing the end of its current IMF program, which has required strict fiscal discipline. Whether Sri Lanka will need to return to the IMF remains an open question. However, the next stage of recovery cannot rely on austerity measures and support from multilateral institutions alone. The key growth reforms include liberalising trade and diversifying the export base, making the tax system more efficient and fair, addressing labour market rigidities, and improving and streamlining FDI regulations. Of these, FDI has become especially pressing in light of recent events.

Much of the policy discussion centres on attracting new investors through roadshows, investment forums and incentive packages. However, less attention is given to an equally important aspect of the FDI story, retaining the investments already secured. Every project that is withdrawn, delayed or stalled sends a powerful signal to the wider market, often speaking far louder than any promotional campaign.

Two recent cases make the point. China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPort) withdrew from its planned $ 392 million logistics hub project at the Port of Colombo in October. Meanwhile, Sinopec’s proposed $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota, considered the largest FDI commitment in Sri Lanka’s history, remains at a standstill despite the signing of the MoU.

Lost opportunity at Colombo Port

On 15 October CMPort exited the commercial and logistics hub project following a mutually agreed settlement with its Sri Lankan partners, Access Engineering, and the Sri Lanka Ports Authority. Established through a joint venture company, the South Asia Commercial and Logistics Hub was envisaged as South Asia’s largest integrated commercial and logistics hub, aimed at strengthening Sri Lanka’s position as a regional trade and maritime centre.

In 2023, an agreement was signed for the construction and operation of the facility under a 50 year Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) arrangement. Under the agreement, CMPort held a 70% stake in the project, while the Sri Lanka Ports Authority and Access Engineering each held 15%.

The decision to withdraw from the investment was driven by concerns relating to the project’s implementation environment, timelines and commercial considerations while some local observers attribute the withdrawal to broader geopolitical pressures. Following the project’s termination, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority has announced plans to develop a new logistics hub through a competitive public private partnership (PPP) model.

It is important to emphasise that CMPort is not leaving Sri Lanka. The company continues to operate the container terminal at the Port of Colombo and remains involved in the Hambantota Port. However, that is precisely the point, when an investor that has already established a long term presence in the country decides to withdraw from a new project, potential investors take notice.

Sinopec’s Hambantota refinery: Biggest deal still on paper

In January 2025, Sri Lanka signed an agreement with Sinopec for a $ 3.7 billion refinery project in Hambantota with a planned processing capacity of 200,000 barrels per day, a significant portion of which is intended for export market. The project is set to represent the largest FDI commitment in the country’s history. For context, Sri Lanka’s only existing refinery at Sapugaskanda has a processing capacity of just 50,000 barrels of crude oil per day.

Despite its scale and strategic significance, the project has made little progress amid a series of unresolved concerns. Mainly the disagreement over market access, with Sinopec seeking unrestricted access to sell its refined products in the local market, while the Government has limited domestic sales to 20% of total output. Additional points of contention include requests for more land, the fiscal concessions available to the investor, and concerns regarding long term water availability in the Hambantota region.


On the issue of local market access, in early 2026, Ministry of Energy stated that Sinopec agreed to proceed with the project under the Government’s 20% cap on domestic fuel sales. At the time, authorities expressed confidence that construction would commence sooner, while also indicating willingness to consider Sinopec’s request for more access to the local fuel market.

However, the project remains on paper, with no clear implementation timeline in place. As a result, the economic benefits associated with the investment continue to be delayed.

What these cases tell us

The two projects differ significantly in scale and sector, yet they share a common pattern. Both were announced with headlines on papers, both encountered obstacles, and both have remained stalled long enough to erode investor confidence.

Getting the fundamentals right from the beginning is essential. The disagreements over land allocation, regulatory clearances and market access surfaced only after agreements had been signed. These are issues that should have been resolved during negotiations. Once a project is announced, investors should have confidence that its core terms and conditions are settled and will not be subject to renegotiation.

Delay carries a cost of its own. Projects that spend years waiting for land allocation, regulatory approvals or final agreements risk losing momentum, missing financing opportunities and weakening internal support from investor’s side. More often than not, prolonged delays inflict more damage on a project than any single obstacle. By the time outstanding issues are resolved, the original investment rationale may no longer exist.

Sri Lanka’s investment story is not written on a paper or promotional campaigns. It is written in the fate of the projects already on the table. A completed refinery in Hambantota or a fully operational logistics hub in Colombo would do far more to attract the next wave of investors than any investment forum or overseas roadshows. 

The priority now should be not only to attract new investment opportunities but also to strengthen investor aftercare. This requires a robust framework centred on a single point of accountability for approved projects, time bound approval processes, and the early and transparent resolution of land, regulatory and policy related issues. Attracting investment is only half the challenge. Retaining it, implementing it and converting commitments into successful projects are what ultimately build a country’s reputation as a credible investment destination.

(The author is a researcher in a leading private investment research firm in Sri Lanka, whose primary focus is researching broader economic issues, including geopolitical/technological developments, and their implications across various sectors with special focus and interest on related developments in China)

title: Why Sri Lanka needs Singapore Temasek-style holding model for SOEs | Daily FT
