Rethinking role of State in business

State-owned enterprises (SOEs) play a significant role in Sri Lanka’s economy. They provide essential services, support national development, generate employment, and manage important public assets. However, the performance of many SOEs has raised serious concerns about financial sustainability, operational efficiency, accountability, and the effective use of public resources. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), in its Country Report No. 23/116, issued in March 2023, identified substantial scope for improving the operational efficiency of Sri Lanka’s State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs).

The fundamental question is not whether the State should own businesses rather than whether the State has the right institutional structure to manage its commercial investments effectively. Sri Lanka needs to move beyond treating SOEs as extensions of Government ministries and begin managing them as professionally governed business enterprises. One possible approach is to establish a Sri Lankan State-owned holding company inspired by Singapore’s Temasek Holdings.

The objective should not be to copy Singapore blindly but it should be to adapt the principles that make the Temasek model valuable pillars of professional ownership, independent boards, commercial discipline, transparent reporting, and long-term value creation. Sri Lanka needs a Government that acts as a responsible owner of businesses, rather than a Government that attempts to run every business through the machinery of administration.

1. Understanding Singapore Temasek model

Temasek Holdings was established in 1974 to own and commercially manage investments and assets previously held by the Singapore Government. Its creation helped separate the Government’s role as a policymaker from its role as a shareholder in commercial enterprises. Today, Temasek is wholly owned by the Singapore Ministry of Finance but operates through its own board and professional management structure. Under the Temasek model, the Government establishes the overall ownership objectives and appoints a competent board. The board, in turn, oversees the company’s strategy, risk management, investments, and senior management. Individual businesses are responsible for their own operational and commercial decisions. The Government does not ordinarily direct individual investment decisions. In simple terms, the model creates a clear separation between three functions:

This arrangement allows commercial enterprises units to operate with greater professional independence while remaining accountable for their results. Temasek is not simply a fund into which the Government deposits money. It owns investments and manages a portfolio of companies with a long-term commercial orientation. It also distributes dividends to its shareholder and publishes information about its performance. The central lesson for Sri Lanka is that public ownership and professional business management do not have to be competing objectives.

2. Why Sri Lanka needs a different approach

Sri Lanka has established numerous public enterprises to support economic development, provide essential services, and protect national interests. Some perform important commercial functions, while others deliver services that the private sector may not provide adequately or affordably. Nevertheless, the performance of SOEs cannot be judged solely by their size, number of employees, or importance to the economy. They must also be evaluated according to their financial results, service quality, productivity, governance, and contribution to national development. Several structural challenges make reform necessary.

2.1 Political interference in commercial decisions

One of the major challenges faced by SOEs was the potential influence of short-term political priorities on long-term business decisions. Frequent changes in leadership, politically influenced appointments, and decisions that do not adequately consider commercial consequences can weaken institutional stability. When business decisions depend on political relationships rather than professional judgement, accountability becomes difficult to establish. A Temasek-style holding company could reduce this risk by introducing transparent board selection criteria, competency-based appointments, fixed performance expectations, and clearly defined responsibilities. Political leaders would retain responsibility for national policy and public ownership objectives, but ordinary commercial decisions would be delegated to professionally appointed boards and management teams.

2.2 Financial losses and the burden on taxpayers

When an SOE repeatedly incurs losses, the consequences extend beyond the enterprise itself. The Government may need to provide additional capital, settle outstanding obligations, restructure debt, or finance essential operations. These resources have an opportunity cost. Money used to support inefficient operations cannot be used for other priorities such as education, healthcare, infrastructure, and social protection. However, not every loss indicates poor management. An enterprise may be required to provide services below commercial cost for legitimate social or economic reasons. The real problem arises when the Government does not clearly distinguish between commercial losses and the cost of fulfilling public-service obligations. Under a reformed model, every enterprise should have an agreed financial and operational mandate. If the Government requires an enterprise to provide a socially necessary service at a loss, the obligation and its cost should be explicitly identified, budgeted, and transparently financed. This would allow management to be held accountable for controllable business performance without unfairly penalising enterprises for Government-imposed obligations.

2.3 Weak accountability and fragmented ownership

SOEs are often subject to multiple layers of oversight involving boards, ministries, departments, Treasury officials, and other public institutions. Although oversight is necessary, fragmented responsibilities can make it difficult to determine who is ultimately accountable for poor performance. A holding company could create a clearer ownership structure. It would establish measurable performance targets, appoint competent boards, monitor results, and take corrective action when enterprises fail to meet agreed objectives. The objective would not be to eliminate public accountability. Instead, it would be to make accountability more meaningful by linking authority, responsibility, and measurable results.

2.4 Limited transparency and inconsistent performance information

Effective reform requires reliable information. The Government, Parliament, investors, employees, and citizens should be able to understand the financial position of major SOEs, their liabilities, government support, operational performance, and contributions to the economy. Sri Lanka has previously pursued performance-management initiatives, including Statements of Corporate Intent for selected SOEs. However, a stronger and more consistent ownership framework is needed to make performance monitoring a regular institutional practice rather than an isolated reform exercise. A holding company should therefore publish audited consolidated financial statements, enterprise-level results, board information, key performance indicators, and details of material Government support. Transparency should be a foundational requirement from the first day of operation.

3. The Proposed solution: Establish “Lanka Holdings”

Sri Lanka could establish a State-owned holding company under a new State Business Enterprises Management Act. For the purposes of this proposal, the institution may be called Lanka Holdings. It would be a public limited company wholly owned by the State, with the Treasury acting as its shareholder. Its principal responsibility would be to manage designated Government-owned commercial investments professionally and maximise their sustainable long-term value. The proposed company should not become another ministry, a regulatory authority, or a central body that micromanages every subsidiary. Instead, it should operate as a professional shareholder with a clear mandate. Its principal functions would include:

1. Holding the State’s shares in designated commercial enterprises.

2. Appointing qualified and independent boards through a transparent selection process.

3. Providing authority to take operational and administrative decisions.

4. Establishing measurable financial, operational, and governance targets.

5. Monitoring the performance and financial risks of subsidiaries.

6. Allocating capital according to commercial viability and national priorities.

7. Publishing audited consolidated accounts and regular performance reports.

8. Receiving dividends and distributing an agreed portion to the treasury.

9. Recommending restructuring, mergers, partnerships, listings, or divestments where appropriate.

The holding company should be subject to parliamentary oversight, independent audit, applicable public disclosure requirements, and clearly defined statutory responsibilities. Its independence must not become an excuse for secrecy or the avoidance of public accountability.

4. Three-tier structure for Sri Lankan SOEs

Sri Lanka should not place every State-owned institution under the same commercial model. Enterprises have different purposes, risks, and obligations. A more practical approach would classify them into three broad categories.

Tier 1: Commercial enterprises

This category would include commercially oriented businesses such as telecommunications, airlines, hotels, plantations, and selected financial or other business enterprises, subject to legal, regulatory, and strategic considerations. Their principal objective should be to generate sustainable financial returns, improve productivity, serve customers, and protect the value of public assets. Each enterprise should operate under a professionally approved business plan with measurable targets for profitability, cash flow, productivity, customer satisfaction, and investment. Where an enterprise is commercially viable, the holding company should support expansion, innovation, partnerships, and access to capital. Where an enterprise remains unviable despite reasonable restructuring, options such as mergers, strategic partnerships, minority listings, or divestment should be evaluated transparently and on their merits. The objective is not to sell public assets indiscriminately. It is to ensure that the State retains ownership where justified and uses its capital efficiently.

Tier 2: Strategic utilities and essential services

Some enterprises provide services that are essential to national security, economic stability, or public welfare. Examples may include Electricity, Petroleum, Railway, and port-related enterprises. These businesses should not be evaluated exclusively on short-term profitability. Their performance should be assessed against a dual mandate of financial sustainability and the delivery of clearly defined public-service obligations. For example, if the Government requires an enterprise to maintain an uneconomic service for social reasons, the cost should be separately calculated and financed through an approved mechanism. This would prevent hidden subsidies from distorting financial results and would help the public understand the true cost of Government policy. Commercial discipline and social responsibility can coexist, provided that both are clearly defined.

Tier 3: Non-core and persistently unviable entities

Sri Lanka should undertake a comprehensive review of smaller, overlapping, inactive, and persistently unviable State-owned entities. Depending on their functions and legal obligations, these enterprises could be merged, consolidated, restructured, transferred, or wound up. A dedicated restructuring unit could coordinate this process using transparent criteria, independent financial assessments, and clearly defined timelines. Before making any decision, the Government must assess employment consequences, contractual commitments, public-service requirements, and the interests of affected stakeholders. Restructuring should be evidence-based, not an automatic exercise in closure or privatisation.

5. Independent Boards and professional leadership

The success of Lanka Holdings would depend less on its name or legal structure than on the quality of its governance. An institution that is formally independent but remains vulnerable to political appointments and informal interference would reproduce the same weaknesses it was designed to address. The holding company should therefore have a predominantly independent board with expertise in finance, corporate governance, strategy, law, risk management, technology, and relevant industry expertise. Board members should be selected through a transparent, competency-based process, with published eligibility criteria, declarations of interests, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. Ministers should not sit on the holding company’s board or the boards of its commercial subsidiaries. Their role should be exercised through the Government’s ownership policy and lawful shareholder mechanisms. The CEO should be appointed through a professional process, with clearly defined responsibilities, an appropriate term of office, and performance-linked remuneration. Appointments and removals should follow established legal procedures, with protection against arbitrary political interference. Each subsidiary board should have genuine authority to supervise its management and make business decisions. The holding company should set strategic expectations and assess results, rather than interfere in routine operational matters. This is the essential difference between a professional holding company and a centralised administrative department.

6. Financial discipline, dividends, and reinvestment

A well-designed holding company should improve the way the State manages the financial resources invested in its enterprises. First, all participating companies should prepare reliable financial statements and disclose material liabilities, guarantees, subsidies, and related-party transactions. Second, the holding company should establish a transparent dividend policy. Profitable enterprises would contribute dividends according to their financial capacity, capital requirements, investment plans, and long-term sustainability. These dividends could provide a more predictable return to the treasury and, ultimately, the public. However, the Government should not extract excessive dividends from enterprises that need capital to maintain infrastructure, modernise operations, or remain competitive. Dividend decisions should balance current public revenue with future enterprise value. Third, capital should be allocated according to transparent investment criteria. Enterprises with credible business plans and strong prospects should be able to compete for investment on merit. Fourth, public enterprises should not be encouraged to accumulate hidden liabilities under the assumption that the treasury will always rescue them.

Government guarantees, where justified, should be explicitly authorised, disclosed, and assessed for fiscal risk. The long-term objective should be to create a cycle in which commercially sound enterprises generate returns, retain sufficient funds for sustainable growth, and contribute appropriately to public finances.

7. Listing on CSE: Option, not objective in itself

A Temasek-style holding structure could create opportunities for carefully selected SOEs to access the capital market. A minority listing could introduce additional disclosure requirements, independent scrutiny, market-based valuation, and broader investor participation. It could also help enterprises raise capital for expansion without relying entirely on Government funding. Nevertheless, listing should not be treated as a substitute for governance reform. An enterprise should not be listed merely to raise immediate revenue or transfer financial risks to private investors. It should first demonstrate credible accounts, appropriate governance, a viable business strategy, and a clear ownership and regulatory framework. Where national interests require the State to retain control, a minority listing could be considered. Where listing is unsuitable, the enterprise could remain wholly State-owned while operating under professional commercial governance. The principle should be simple “Reform governance first, establish credibility next, and consider market participation when the conditions are right.”

8. Lessons from SEMA and previous reform attempts

Sri Lanka’s previous institutional reform experiences offer an important warning. The establishment of another authority or restructuring institution does not, by itself, guarantee sustainable reform. An institution may lose effectiveness if it lacks a clear mandate, consistent political support, operational independence, or the authority needed to implement its responsibilities. The proposed Lanka Holdings must therefore be designed to avoid becoming another institution that exists on paper but has limited influence over actual SOE performance. Its mandate should be established by legislation, with clear limits on political intervention and transparent rules governing board appointments, reporting, capital allocation, and restructuring decisions. The law should also define the circumstances in which the Government can issue lawful directions and require such directions to be documented and disclosed, subject to legitimate confidentiality and national-security requirements. At the same time, no statutory arrangement can eliminate political interference entirely. Strong institutions require enforcement, a professional public service, independent oversight, and sustained public commitment. Sri Lanka should learn from earlier reform attempts by building safeguards into the institutional design rather than relying on assurances of good intentions.

9. Protecting public assets and workers’ interests

SOE reform must be approached as a national economic and governance reform, not simply as a cost-cutting programme. Employees have legitimate concerns about job security, working conditions, statutory payments, career development, and fair treatment. These concerns should be addressed through consultation, transparent restructuring plans, skills development, redeployment where feasible, and legally compliant employment arrangements. Workers’ retirement savings, including the Employees’ Provident Fund (EPF) and Employees’ Trust Fund (ETF), should not be treated as a convenient source of capital for the holding company. Any involvement of these funds in investment activities must remain subject to their own legal mandates, fiduciary duties, and independent governance. Similarly, public assets should not be transferred or sold without proper valuation, due diligence, disclosure, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. A successful reform programme must demonstrate that better governance benefits the country as a whole, not only investors or the treasury.

10. Practical five-year implementation roadmap

Sri Lanka should introduce the proposed model gradually, with measurable milestones and independent evaluation.

Years 1–2: Establish the foundations

Years 3–4: Expand and strengthen

Year 5 onwards: Consolidate and create long-term value

Progress should be measured through improvements in financial sustainability, productivity, service quality, transparency, capital efficiency, and the reduction of unjustified fiscal risks not simply by the number of enterprises transferred or privatised.

11. Can Sri Lanka replicate Singapore’s success?

Sri Lanka should recognise that Temasek operates within a different institutional and economic environment. Singapore’s experience cannot be separated from its governance arrangements, professional capabilities, regulatory framework, and long-term policy consistency. Consequently, establishing a holding company will not automatically make Sri Lankan SOEs profitable. If the same political appointment practices, weak reporting systems, and informal interventions continue under a new institutional name, the reform will achieve little. Sri Lanka must first establish credible ownership rules, independent boards, transparent accounts, enforceable performance targets, and effective oversight. It must also accept that some enterprises may require fundamental restructuring, while others may be commercially viable if their governance and operating arrangements improve. The objective should not be to promise that every SOE will generate profits. It should be to ensure that every SOE has a clearly justified purpose, an accountable management structure, a transparent financial position, and a measurable contribution to the country.

Conclusion: From political ownership to professional stewardship

Sri Lanka’s SOE challenge is fundamentally a governance challenge. The country needs to move from fragmented administrative control towards professional, transparent, and accountable ownership of its commercial public assets. A Singapore Temasek-style holding company could provide an institutional framework for this transformation. By separating policymaking from commercial ownership, strengthening independent boards, introducing financial discipline, and making performance visible to the public, Sri Lanka could improve the management of its State-owned businesses and reduce unnecessary fiscal pressures. 

However, the proposed model should not be regarded as a shortcut to economic recovery. It must be supported by sound legislation, credible institutions, professional leadership, transparent financial reporting, and consistent implementation. The ultimate purpose is not merely to increase profits or collect dividends. It is to protect the value of public assets, improve the quality of essential services, encourage productive investment, and ensure that the State’s commercial resources contribute more effectively to national development.

(The author holds a DBA (Reading), MBA in HRM, Pg Dip in HRM, Pg Dip in Def.Mgt, BBA in HRM, Assoc CIPD(UK), AMCIPM(SL) and was Deputy General Manager (HR & Administration) at Sri Lanka State Plantations Corporations)

title: From street Bhandiwalla to $ 624 b Circular Economy: How South Asian tradition can power sustainable growth | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:21
-     - 45

Addressing the Regional Forum on Circular Economy – South Asia, jointly organised by SAARC and the Federation of Chambers of Commerce and Industry of Sri Lanka (FCCISL) with support from the Institute for Global Environmental Strategies (IGES), brought back a vivid memory from my childhood in Mumbai.

Echoing down the street outside our apartment, a vendor carrying a large basket on his head would call out: “Bhandiwalla, Bhandiwalla!” Once or twice a year, my mother would call him upstairs. He would unload his basket to reveal sparkling stainless-steel utensils. My mother would bring out a stack of old, worn-out family clothes, and the bargaining would begin. Eventually, they would settle on a fair barter—a gleaming steel plate, bowl, or glass in exchange for a pile of discarded garments.

That street vendor was a key operator in a thriving, decentralised circular economy. He took those old clothes and systematically repurposed them. Usable garments were cleaned, ironed, and resold in smaller towns and villages. Hardware like buttons and zips were salvaged and sold to local tailors. Nothing was wasted; everything was reused, repurposed, or recycled. Landfills simply did not factor into the equation.

A philosophy embedded in cultural DNA

This informal barter system was not merely a survival tactic; it was the practical manifestation of an ancient South Asian worldview. The Indian philosophy of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam (“the world is one family”) highlights the intrinsic interdependence of all living beings. Similarly, the concept of Ahimsa—practiced so powerfully by Mahatma Gandhi—demands non-violence not only toward human beings but also implicitly toward the natural environment.

At South Asian dining tables, children are raised with a fundamental command: never waste a single morsel of food. In our culture, squandering resources is viewed almost as a moral failing.

While the modern global economy operates largely on a linear “take-make-dispose” model, the circular economy focuses on “use, repurpose, renew, and recycle.” It ensures materials remain continuously within the economic loop rather than ending up as toxic land contamination.

Entrepreneurial communities: South Asia’s original circular pioneers

While India’s current position as one of the world’s fastest-growing major economies is frequently attributed to its demographic dividend, its bedrock lies in entrenched entrepreneurial communities. Long before modern sustainability frameworks were codified, these merchant networks jumpstarted trade by operationalising zero-waste principles:

The Marwaris (Rajasthan) and operational efficiency: Marwari trade culture was built on eliminating operational leakage (kasar). In early merchant supply chains, packaging materials—dunnage, burlap sacks, wooden crates, and metal bindings—were systematically harvested, graded, and resold across secondary commodity markets. Machinery in Marwari-run mills was continuously repaired, retrofitted, and downgraded through secondary manufacturing tiers before final scrap recovery. Furthermore, through community banking instruments (Hundis), financial capital circulated internally, minimising interest leakage to external institutions.

Nattukottai Chettiars (Tamil Nadu) and cross-border loops: As maritime merchant bankers operating across South and Southeast Asia, the Chettiars optimised cross-border shipping networks. Vessels exporting spices or textiles never returned empty; they brought back timber, stone, and raw materials as structural ballast, which were immediately converted into construction materials upon arrival.

Gujaratis and Jains (Western India) and material valorisation: Guided by Ahimsa, these trading guilds prioritised resource stewardship. Gujarati networks pioneered secondary textile markets by collecting cotton mill waste (ru) and processing short-staple fibers into coarse industrial cloth, paper, or stuffing. This ethos also built major industrial salvage hubs like Alang in Gujarat, where decommissioned ships are systematically stripped down to re-roll structural steel and re-introduce every component back into the industrial supply chain.

Parsis (Mumbai and Gujarat) and extended lifespan design: Industrial pioneers like the Tata and Godrej families rejected planned obsolescence. Heavy consumer products—from steel cabinetry and locks to industrial machinery—were engineered for multi-generational durability, modular repair, and high residual scrap value. Moreover, industrial profits were systematically reinvested into urban green belts, housing trusts, and civic infrastructure.

Bunts (Coastal Karnataka) and integrated agro-hospitality loops: In traditional Bunt-run restaurant networks (such as Udupi eateries), organic kitchen waste was redirected to coastal dairy farms or converted into agricultural compost. In native Canara agricultural estates, every component of coconut and arecanut cultivation was monetised—husks became coir fiber, fronds were woven into roofing, shells were converted into activated carbon, and fallen leaves served as biodegradable serving plates (patravali).

Modern start-ups harnessing waste for wealth

This ancestral ingenuity is currently experiencing a high-tech revival across South Asia’s start-up ecosystem:

Chakr Innovation has developed the “Chakr Shield,” a technology that captures particulate matter emissions from diesel generators and converts it into high-grade industrial ink—now purchased by global tech firms like Dell.

Boson White Water addresses industrial water security by treating sewage effluent from large apartment complexes to potable standards for use in IT parks and industrial facilities. In an era of booming data center expansion, such liquid waste innovations are vital.

The scale of the crisis

Despite these deep-rooted traditions and promising innovations, South Asia faces an unprecedented environmental challenge driven by rapid urbanisation:

1. Surging Solid Waste: India’s urban population is projected to reach 600 million (40%) by 2030 and 800 million by 2050. Consequently, annual municipal solid waste (MSW) generation will surge from roughly 62 million tons today to 165 million tons by 2030, and 436 million tons by 2050.

2. Urban Land Loss: Unmanaged dumping currently locks up over 10,000 hectares of prime urban land across 2,100+ legacy dumpsites (such as Delhi’s Ghazipur and Okhla mounds), posing serious public health hazards.

3. Unused Liquid Waste: India generates 112 billion litres of domestic wastewater daily (the 3rd largest volume globally), but only ~28% undergoes treatment. Monetising treated urban wastewater for industrial and agricultural reuse represents a potential ₹3.04 trillion market opportunity by 2047.

4. Resource Dependencies: Urban material consumption is set to more than double—from 40 billion tons in 2010 to 90 billion tons by 2050. Heavily reliant on imported critical minerals for electronics, electric vehicles (EVs), and heavy manufacturing, the region urgently requires urban mining and closed-loop recycling networks to secure strategic supply chain autonomy.

The macroeconomic opportunity

Where there is a resource crisis, there is tremendous macroeconomic potential. Joint research by the Ellen MacArthur Foundation and NITI Aayog reveals that transitioning to a circular economy could unlock ₹40 lakh crore ($624 billion) in annual value for India by 2050—equivalent to 30% of its current GDP.

In the near term, adopting circular practices across construction, agriculture, mobility, and manufacturing could yield ₹14 lakh crore ($218 billion) in annual material cost savings by 2030, lowering production costs by 11% while creating millions of skilled and semi-skilled green jobs across formal and informal sectors.

Bridging tradition and tomorrow

The path forward for South Asia does not require importing alien economic philosophies. The core tenets of the circular economy are already encoded in our cultural history, our childhood memories of the bhandiwalla, and our traditional business networks.

By combining modern technology and regulatory frameworks with our ancestral values of resource stewardship and non-wastage, South Asia can transform its urban waste challenges into a powerful engine for job creation, sustainable growth, and long-term economic prosperity.

(The author is the President of the Lanka India Business Association (LIBA). He can be reached at santoshmenon1@me.com)

title: Skyscrapers on a quagmire | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 28 October 2026 00:20
-     - 47

On 21 October, the developers of PHP – the engine behind around 70% of the world’s websites – disclosed 2 severe flaws, since nicknamed PHP2Shell, that could let a stranger with no password take control of the computer behind a website. The US National Security Agency then told organisations unable to fix their systems to take them offline, and the South African Presidency, the Finnish Government and the UK Government did exactly that within hours, if not days. Sri Lankans got a general advisory from SL-CERT the same day, naming no institution. Not a single site was taken offline.

Over next 3 days that followed I checked around 640 live gov.lk sites I could discover. I was searching for critical PHP vulnerabilities, but came back with a far more disturbing picture of, and appreciation for the incredible fragility of our public digital, and critical national infrastructure.

80 vulnerable sites, and likely much more

At least 80 websites run by the state, or by the utilities and companies it owns, run vulnerable versions of PHP, and 61 of them run versions so old that the makers stopped fixing them years ago, which means they carry every flaw discovered since and have no official repair available. This isn’t a complete number since for a lot of technical reasons, including by measures established to thwart potential hackers, it’s often impossible to determine specific vulnerabilities that exist within websites as an outsider. Accordingly, I could only count sites that announced their software version.

The list reads like an organisational chart of the state, running from the Ceylon Electricity Board and the Disaster Management Centre, both on a version released in June 2013, through LECO, the Sri Lanka Ports Authority, SLT Mobitel, the Telecommunications Regulatory Commission, the National Transport Commission, the Sri Lanka Air Force and the Department for Registration of Persons, which holds the national identity card registry, to the Ministries of Health, Mass Media and Justice, a Prime Minister’s Office system, the Bribery Commission, the Department of Government Information, the National Police Commission, 8 of the 9 provinces, 3 municipal councils and several Pradeshiya Sabhas. These are not random or peripheral sites.

Worse still, the Ministry of Health’s human resources systems, which handle transfers, post-intern appointments and appeals for health workers, run on a version released in July 2010, while a ministry portal asks doctors to log in with their national identity card numbers, and the Bribery Commission takes complaints from the public, so NIC numbers, employment records and the details of those who report corruption all sit behind architectures no one has updated or maintained in years.

It truly beggars belief.

The rot beyond PHP

Updating PHP won’t fix what ails many official websites. 9 state sites, including the CEB and the Air Force, publish diagnostic pages that display their entire server configuration to anyone who looks, and the login pages of database administration tools, which are by definition doors to databases, are reachable on the Sri Lanka Police, Ministry of Defence, Disaster Management Centre and LECO sites, with LECO’s dating from 2017. The Railway Department, the Auditor General’s Department and the Director General of Merchant Shipping share a server whose public status page leaks the address of a machine inside the Government network, while a Pradeshiya Sabha site briefly exposed the kind of file that typically holds passwords and keys. The Auditor General’s Department, whose job is to hold the rest of the state to account, is amongst them. 

Other countries try their best to secure this sensitive information by layer upon layer of safeguards, including regular updates to the underlying code. The situation in Sri Lanka is vastly different, and stolen data held to crypto-currency ransoms we simply can’t afford to pay may actually be the least of our worries. In a country with a long and recent history of disinformation driving offline violence, a compromised official website is the most credible vehicle for falsehood imaginable. A forged flood warning on the Disaster Management Centre’s site during a cyclone, or a false tariff notice on the CEB’s, would be believed precisely because of where it appeared. Nor do attackers usually stop at the website. Once they control it, they can use it as a way into the databases and internal Government networks that sit behind it.

Gmail, the Fuel Pass and a culture of convenience

The state of our servers are a symptom of absolutely rotten institutional cultures decades in the making. In March I wrote about the National Fuel Pass, whose rollout failed to recognise newly issued NIC numbers, sent one-time passwords after they had expired and showed second-hand vehicles under their previous owners, while for over 48 hours no ministry or development team said anything online, leaving Asela Waidyalankara, an independent cybersecurity expert, to field public complaints on Twitter/X, and act as a conduit to the authorities. 

You couldn’t make it up. 

Earlier this month, I went through the first 500 search results for gmail.com (the commercial Gmail domain) on official gov.lk domains. I found state bodies advertising consumer Gmail addresses for right-to-information requests, procurement, health appointments and child protection, with the Department of Census and Statistics directing confidential survey returns to district addresses, many of them Gmail, and the Registrar General’s website displaying an official address whose link opens a Gmail one.

Consumer Gmail accounts leave citizens’ identity, health and bank details dependent on whoever holds the password, with no institutional control over custody, retention or continuity when staff move on. All this, with the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA) becoming fully operational on 1 January 2027. I have yet to hear the President, or Dr. Hans Wijayasuriya as Chief Presidential Adviser on Digital Economy, speak to any of it.

Photo-opportunities vs ground realities

The public are regularly shown photographs of meetings with the Indian High Commissioner, the UN system, the World Bank and other bilateral and multilateral partners about funding or supporting digitalisation, from the Sri Lanka Unique Digital Identity scheme to GovPay, whereas the rot in the foundations these platforms are being retrofitted onto, and the cultures that produced it, never feature. Nor does the fact that no single body is mandated to keep the state’s systems current, since SL-CERT can advise institutions but cannot compel them, as Deputy Minister of Digital Economy Eranga Weeraratne told Parliament in March 2025, and as late as May 2026 no law required institutions to report incidents to it.

Countries that have more successfully address this Gordian Knot of issues have established a dedicated institution, with a clear mandate for 5 years or more, with the people, processes and regulatory authority to build what was missing, and not just by issuing advisories. The expertise to help exists, including within the UN system, if the Government asks for it directly, and means it. It may be that the President, Deputy Minister Weeraratne, and Dr. Wijayasuriya somewhat grasp the problem. But the true state of even critical national infrastructure suggests they may under-appreciate how fundamentally flawed the foundations really are, including beyond Government. 

Infrastructure this brittle can quickly turn any small, sustained shock into a major socio-economic, and political crisis – and we are sitting ducks.

Parliament’s blind spot

Earlier this month, I published a report on a study of 173 Hansards, from January 2025 to September 2026, focussing on digitalisation, and AI. MPs did discuss cybersecurity, and often in ways that bear out what I found last week. Ajith P. Perera pressed for cybersecurity legislation in drafting since 2019, Chathura Galappaththi urged a security framework and bug-bounty testing before any biometric data is collected, and Ravi Karunanayake sought a forensic audit after the October 2025 Lanka Government Cloud disruption, which the Deputy Minister attributed to a full disk on a platform with no centralised backup. The Deputy Minister later told the House that the 2023 ransomware attack permanently erased emails linked to around 5,000 Government addresses because institutions lacked offline backups, and in August 2026 the Leader of the Opposition cited weak passwords and missing multi-factor authentication behind the US$2.5 million lost during a debt repayment to Australia. The floor debate, though, was around fraud, deepfakes and online harms rather than the upkeep of the state’s own systems. MPs need to better understand ground realities – software unpatched for decades, exposed private data – as well as emergent developments, where AI makes finding, and exploiting vulnerabilities cheaper, faster, more automated, and available to anyone, anywhere. The resulting risks, threats, and harms to Sri Lanka will grow exponentially.

Foundations before facades

We are being promised skyscrapers built on quagmires. 

The fixes are unglamorous, but urgent. They include, but aren’t limited to a complete inventory of state systems with a named official accountable for each, and a binding rule that institutions run only supported software. Every second more with foundations this fragile, and institutional cultures this frightful invites a collective national grief we can ill afford after 2022.

title: SLC cuts down on franchise cricket | Daily FT

By Sa’adi Thawfeeq

One of the teething problems that Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC) has failed to address is the influx of national cricketers frequently going and playing franchise cricket around the world at the cost of national interest.

This has resulted in players picked for a certain tour arriving straight from playing franchise cricket instead of being part of the tour squad and undergoing training as one unit. It has also resulted in the question of fitness of such players and subsequently the injuries they suffer, which is detrimental to the national team’s interest.

“We felt that at one stage playing for Sri Lanka is like getting your foot into different franchises,” said SLC Transformation Committee member Sidath Wettimuny.

“We want to change that perception and we are going to bring about a rule where we will say 10 days before a national tour you’ve got to be with the squad back home. Plus, we are going to restrict franchise cricket to a maximum of three which includes the LPL (Lanka Premier League). Depending on the fitness etc. a cricketer can play in two more franchises if SLC gives an NOC (No Objection Certificate) to play.”

“For example, for the recent England tour, four of our players came from the West Indies, two days before the tour commenced. We are going to stop that. We are going to restrict the players to the 8 main franchises. The players’ contracts end shortly this year in their new contracts. We’ll make sure that regulation is there. We want to rationalize the whole process for the players to make sure that Sri Lanka cricket is the priority. Playing franchise cricket is well and good but their priority must be to represent the country.”

Transformation Committee chairman Eran Wickramaratne addressing the media at their monthly meeting said that there was no issue with the ICC funding of SLC although at present, it is run by a government appointed body.

“We have the support of the ICC in what we are doing. They can see that we are in the process of putting good governance in place. The ICC has its own regulations and how they administer it. The funds are coming, the methods have changed,” said Wickramaratne.

“What we are focusing on as a committee is not only on receiving funds, we are very focused on how the funds are being spent. That’s very critical and important. We are focused on what our priorities are in spending those funds?

“We are very much focused on waste management and basically saving every single rupee so that it can be put into school cricket, to women’s cricket and cricket in general. We are focused on having pre-evaluation particularly when it comes to capital expenditure. I don’t like saying this, but just to illustrate the point we have floodlights here (at the SSC). These floodlights have cost us more than Rs. 1.7 billion. Since the installation of these floodlights only one match has been played. When we get into capital expenditure we will do very careful evaluation in terms of financial returns. We are there to play cricket, but we are there to play cricket intelligently.”

Wickramaratne also revealed that they have begun a reserve fund for SLC from this month.

On the question of at which stage the new SLC constitution stood at the present moment, Wickramaratne replied, “The Supreme Court will most likely provide its verdict and conclusion this week. Then it will be tabled in Parliament the following week. After that, a debate could be called in Parliament for a second reading of the bill and a vote could be taken. We think that process should be concluded approximately a month from now. But certainly this year we will see the new constitution become law on SLC. After that it will take several weeks to implement it because there are elected officials and appointed officials that have to go through a process.”    

Transformation Committee member Roshan Mahanama appearing for the first time at a media conference said, “If anyone wants to be an elite athlete you cannot compromise on discipline and fitness.”

Speaking on a few key areas that the committee has started to develop Mahanama named, match officiating from grass root levels, a curator with a good background, appointment of coaches, restructuring of the entire High Performance Centre (HPC), a brain centre where ‘we are about 10 years behind other countries’, bringing in a cricket season which is important for workload management, injury recovery, technical challenges, an accreditation policy for player-managers, a women’s protection policy, a child safe-guarding and a child protection policy ‘’as we have under 17 boys and under 19 girls (some of them are 15 years)’.

Infrastructure proposals include an international-standard stadium, wider facilities across the island and football grounds in every district, with work on the latter expected to begin next year. Separately, the FFSL plans to develop around 40 grounds through its member leagues by the end of 2031, according to the program outlined.

title: Kane, Putellas crowned Ballon d’Or winners | Daily FT

Harry Kane (right) and Alexia Putellas

England captain Harry Kane and Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas have been crowned the world’s best players at the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London. Kane is the first English player to win the men’s award since Michael Owen in 2001, and Putellas has won the Ballon d’Or Feminin for a record-equalling third time.

Kane, 33, is the fifth Englishman to win the Ballon d’Or, after Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966), Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) and Owen. Scotland’s Denis Law (1964) and Northern Ireland’s George Best (1968) are the only other winners from the United Kingdom. Kane is also the first Bayern Munich player to win since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981. Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal was third.

Putellas, 32, collected the most votes from an international panel of journalists across FIFA’s top 50 ranked countries. Barcelona striker Ewa Pajor finished second and Manchester City forward Khadija Shaw third. Putellas draws level with Spain teammate and former Barcelona colleague Aitana Bonmati, who won in 2023, 2024 and 2025 after Putellas’ wins in 2021 and 2022. The pair have won the past six awards, with Norway’s Ada Hegerberg (2018) and Megan Rapinoe of the United States (2019) the only non-Spanish winners.

Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most by a Bayern player in a single campaign. Only one player at a club in Europe’s top five leagues has ever scored more in a season. Including England matches, he scored 73 goals and provided eight assists in 65 games. He won the award despite missing out on football’s biggest prizes, after losing in the semi-finals of both the World Cup and the Champions League.

Putellas captained Barcelona to the Champions League title as part of a quadruple in 2025-26, before joining Women’s Super League (WSL) side London City Lionesses in July. Her win caps a return to the top of world football after a career-threatening anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) knee injury in 2022.

“I had to go through many ups and downs, especially early in my career. I was never the person that people thought was going to be the superstar like some of the guys now,” Kane told DAZN. “I had to bide my time and work hard. A lot of times it was me against my own mind, and I had to come through it. I had to show self-belief and determination.”

“Don’t listen if someone tells you that you can’t do it. Believe in yourself,” Putellas said.

England Manager Thomas Tuchel said he was ‘delighted’ by Kane’s win and hailed it as a ‘huge honour’, while Prince William described the former Tottenham Hotspur player as a ‘brilliant captain’ and ‘remarkable player’. The Wembley arches were lit up in gold on Monday night to mark the win.

This combination of strength, control and reliability makes the Mitsubishi Triton (L200) double cab ideally suited to Sri Lanka’s varied driving conditions — from city roads and highways to plantations, construction sites and challenging off-road environments.
